setup: At a parcel counter, a clerk’s airline cancelled her flight. She declined replacement travel, so DOT’s rule requires an automatic refund. It sent a voucher instead. She offers $8 to sort return labels while she reads the rule. Her cash drawer refuses to recognize the voucher as a relative.

choices.label: Read the refund rule with her
choices.outcome: You confirm that the refund must use her original payment method. “I paid with money,” she says. “Apparently that was an unusual choice.”

effects.log: You confirm that the refund must use her original payment method. “I paid with money,” she says. “Apparently that was an unusual choice.”

choices.label: Sort return labels for $8
choices.outcome: You sort the labels, earn $8 and rest your aching eyes. The drawer produces cash on its first attempt. She wonders whether it has airline-management experience.

effects.log: You sort the labels, earn $8 and rest your aching eyes. The drawer produces cash on its first attempt. She wonders whether it has airline-management experience.

choices.label: Skip the job
choices.outcome: You leave unpaid and annoyed. She folds the unwanted voucher into a paper plane. At last, something this airline sent her can take off.

effects.log: You leave unpaid and annoyed. She folds the unwanted voucher into a paper plane. At last, something this airline sent her can take off.

sources.title: DOT: What passengers need to know about the automatic refund rule
sources.qualification: Eligibility and timing rules apply; not every delay warrants a refund. The parcel clerk’s cancelled flight, rejected alternative and unwanted voucher are fiction, not an allegation about a named airline.
sources.claim: DOT’s rule requires automatic refunds when an airline cancels or significantly changes a flight and the passenger declines replacement travel or other offered compensation. Refunds must use the original payment method.

title: The direct route is closed
setup: Treasury suspended the IRS’s free Direct File tool for 2026; other free filing options remain. At a used-computer stall, a seller offers $12 to sort replacement labels for old tax-help kiosks. The machines still work. Only the part where government made itself convenient has broken.

choices.label: Sort the replacement labels for $12
choices.outcome: You earn $12 and a headache sorting “Direct File” from “Other filing options.” The computers pass every hardware test. The government needs a replacement part.

effects.log: You earn $12 and a headache sorting “Direct File” from “Other filing options.” The computers pass every hardware test. The government needs a replacement part.

choices.label: Preserve the old and new captions
choices.outcome: You save both captions and the IRS update, head aching. The seller keeps one old label: “File directly with us.” Apparently that was the experimental feature.

effects.log: You save both captions and the IRS update, head aching. The seller keeps one old label: “File directly with us.” Apparently that was the experimental feature.

choices.label: Get back on the road
choices.outcome: You leave the job behind. He puts the empty kiosks on sale. “Taxes still mandatory,” he calls. “Helpful government sold separately.”

sources.title: GAO B-337954: Suspension of IRS Direct File
sources.qualification: The GAO decision addresses Congressional Review Act procedure, not whether suspending the service was good policy. No claim that all free filing vanished, that all alternatives charge fees, or that the government sold any real kiosks.
sources.claim: Treasury suspended IRS Direct File in fall 2025, and the IRS confirmed it would not be available for the 2026 filing season. Other free filing programs, including IRS Free File, remain.
